hook: The prince who sent Portugal's ships into the unknown Atlantic.

pages.x: Henry was the third son of King John I of Portugal and his English queen, Philippa. In 1415, aged 21, he helped capture Ceuta, a Muslim port in North Africa, where he heard of gold caravans crossing the Sahara from lands far to the south.

From the south-west tip of Portugal, near Sagres, he paid for voyage after voyage down the coast of Africa. He gathered mapmakers, sailors and shipbuilders, though he never sailed on the voyages himself. His sailors settled Madeira and the Azores, where sugar soon made Portugal rich.
His shipbuilders developed the caravel, a small, light ship with triangular sails that could sail close into the wind.
pages.fx: Caravels could explore unknown coasts and beat their way home against the wind. They opened the age of discovery; Columbus crossed the Atlantic in two of them.

pages.x: Sailors dreaded Cape Bojador on the Sahara coast, where the sea was said to boil and sea monsters waited. For years Henry's captains turned back. In 1434 his squire Gil Eanes finally sailed round it, and found only calm water.

In 1444 his ships brought 235 captured Africans to Lagos, in Portugal, and sold them. It was the start of the Atlantic slave trade. A chronicler who watched wrote that even he wept to see families torn apart.

Henry never sailed farther than North Africa, but the voyages he paid for began Europe's age of exploration. They led to Vasco da Gama's route to India and a Portuguese empire around the world, and also to the Atlantic slave trade.
